Canada online casinos are legal to play at in every province, but the market splits sharply in how it's run. Ontario and Alberta let private operators compete for your business under a full suite of provincial license, while the rest of the country still routes everything through a single government platform.
We track more than 70 real money sites across Canada and rank them by game selection, banking speed, and how each province's regulator handles licensing, refreshed for 2026. If you're after the best online casino in Canada for your specific province, start with the rankings below, then check how winnings get taxed and what keeps your account secure.

Fanatics receives an AGCO license August 11 to run sportsbook and casino in Ontario, its first market outside the U.S. The brand is not live yet and still needs an operating agreement with iGaming Ontario before it can take bets.
July 2026
Alberta's regulated iGaming market goes live July 13, making it Canada's second competitive online gambling province after Ontario. 22 operator sites launch on day one against the government-run Play Alberta platform, with the AGLC as regulator and the AiGC handling commercial agreements.
Hard Rock Bet launches in Ontario July 22, its first market outside the U.S. The debut pairs a full sportsbook with 3,000-plus casino games and makes Hard Rock the province's 48th licensed operator, roughly two months after clearing AGCO registration.
June 2026
Ontario's BetGuard self-exclusion platform goes live across all 82 regulated iGaming sites. Players 19+ can opt out of every licensed operator through a single registration at BetGuard.ca, with terms ranging from six months to a custom duration.
40+ Alberta operators have paid their AGLC registration fees ahead of the July 13 market launch, covering global brands and Canadian-owned platforms, with River Cree iGaming the only Alberta land-based operator in the mix.
Ontario stayed the country's largest regulated market, posting a CA$27.8B Q1 2026 handle across 50-plus operators as the AGCO moved toward its Centralized Self-Exclusion launch.
May 2026
Alberta's July 13 launch continues to build momentum. Three game suppliers secured AGLC licenses this month alone, with Play'n GO the latest on May 26, joining Gaming Corps (May 12) and EveryMatrix (May 19).
Ontario's AGCO continues advancing its Centralized Self-Exclusion (CSE) program, targeting a mid-2026 launch that will let players opt out of all licensed operators through a single registration.
April 2026
Over 33 iGaming applications are in process to go live in Alberta. theScore Bet becomes the latest operator to receive formal AGLC registration approval ahead of the July 13 launch.
Ontario's AGCO updates its iGaming standards ahead of the CSE launch, requiring all operators to integrate with the centralized system and maintain dual exclusion tools for at least 12 months post-launch.
March 2026
Caesars Entertainment opens pre-registration in Alberta with three platforms: Caesars Palace Online Casino, Caesars Sportsbook and Casino, and Horseshoe.
iGaming Alberta confirms July 13 as the go-live date and hard deadline for grey-market operators to cease activity or face permanent exclusion from the province.
February 2026
Ontario's AGCO proposes a five-day suspension of PointsBet Canada's gaming license, citing a failure to detect and report suspicious betting patterns tied to the Jontay Porter NBA scandal. PointsBet contests the ruling, calling it disproportionate to an isolated incident of human error.
Ontario's Ad Standards body begins accepting complaints under the new Canadian Code for Advertising of Gambling, adding a new layer of oversight to operator marketing practices.
January 2026
Alberta introduces the regulatory framework to launch a commercial iGaming market, positioning the province to become only the second in Canada after Ontario to allow private online casino operators.
iGaming Ontario reports a record CA$9.5 billion in total wagers for January 2026, a 21.4% year-over-year increase, as Ontario's regulated market continues to grow across all operators.
Who Oversees the Market For Casino Gaming in Canada?
Canada's federal Criminal Code is the primary governing body in the Great WhiteNorth that oversees gambling activity online with additional help from the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC).
Regulation and oversight when it comes to dealing with operators and residents, however, is primarily set at the province level.

Is it legal to play online Canadian casinos?
+
Yes, it's legal to play casinos online across all of Canada's 10 provinces.
How many provinces in Canada have a regulated casino market online?
+
Currently the only regulated online casino markets are Alberta and Ontario. Alberta launched their own regulated market with private operators this summer on July 13. BC, Quebec, Manitoba, and the Atlantic provinces all have a government run platform.
What does "Rest of Canada" mean?
+
Rest of Canada references all the provinces outside of Alberta and Ontario. Since those provinces both have regulated online casino markets, the rest of Canada includes all the provinces without a regulated online casino market. All rest of Canada markets allow online casinos to operate within their province though none hold licenses to operate within the province, meaning you don't get the same consumer protections that you would in Alberta or Ontario.
Can tourists gamble in Canada?
+
Yes, tourists can gamble while in Canada.
What's the latest province in Canada to launch regulated online casinos?
+
Alberta is the latest province in Canada to launch a regulated online casino market. Casinos went online in a regulated framework on July 13, 2026, launching with over 20 casinos online on day 1.
Are there any no-verification casinos in Canada?
+
No. You must verify your identity at each regulated online casino across Canada. Rest of Canada casinos are the same; to deposit and play you must verify you're eligible to wager at casinos online.
Why do some Canadian provinces offer dozens of casino brands while some only have one?
+
Two provinces, Ontario and Alberta, have regulated markets where they allow for private operators to offer their casinos. Other rest of Canada provinces have a government-ran brand with offshore casinos not legal or illegal to operate in the province.
Can I use a VPN to play on Ontario or Alberta's regulated casino sites from another province?
+
No, and you shouldn't do that. Spoofing your location with a VPN will breach the operator's terms, and if it's caught, your account gets frozen with your balance stuck inside it. Ontario requires registered operators to confirm a player is physically located in the province before letting them play, and that holds even if the account itself is based in Ontario; anyone outside the province isn't permitted to take part. Alberta's AGLC-licensed apps run the same location check.
